course.title: Hacking Hybrid Course
course.lead: Twelve ordered days through the security books on this laptop, each naming the exact pages, carrying a bite of the author's words, and ending at a runnable local exercise. Defensive scope only: you are learning to find and fix weaknesses, with authorization, on systems you own or are permitted to test.
course.method: Same rhythm as the ML branch: **recall** → **read the author** → **practice** (run the exercise, predict output first) → **check**. Review days re-test earlier ideas at 1, 3, 7 and 21 lessons back. Nothing here authorizes testing a system you do not own or have written permission to test.
course.teacher_basis: Fields follow the local SyncSenta teacher schema (outcome, prerequisite, expected misconception, assessment evidence) from `Sync-0.0.2/data/ai_curriculum.json`, adapted for an adult self-learner.

books.author: Roberto Ghibaut Llorente et al.
books.note: 515 pages of tooling. Headings were not machine-detectable, so use it as the lab reference a day points into, rather than a spine source.

days.title: What a hacker actually does, and what the law says
days.idea: Hacking is applying deep understanding of a system to an unintended purpose; the difference between crime and profession is written authorization and scope.
days.recall: From memory, name the three roles (black hat, white hat, grey hat) and say which one you are training to be, and why scope documents exist.
days.misconception: Believing permission is implied because a system is reachable, or because it is a test lab you found online.
days.practice: Open `../security-exercises/exercises/00_scope/01_authorized_target.py`. It only accepts targets on an explicit allow-list and makes no network call — that guard **is** the lesson. Implement it, then run `python3 ../security-exercises/run_tests.py`.
days.check: Your scope statement must name at least one asset that is explicitly OUT of scope. Evidence: the file path in your log.
days.gate: Explain, without the page, why a scanner sweep of a neighbour's network is unlawful even when nothing is damaged.

days.title: The five phases of an attack, in order
days.idea: Reconnaissance → scanning → gaining access → maintaining access → covering tracks; a penetration test follows the same order and stops where the contract stops.
days.practice: No code today. Read `../security-exercises/README.md` and write one line in your log mapping each of the 13 exercises to the phase it belongs to. That table is your model of the phases.
days.check: Day 1 recall (1 back). Write the five phases from memory before opening anything.
days.gate: Given a fictional contract, say which of the five phases are permitted and which are not, with reasons.

days.title: Information gathering before you touch a host
days.idea: Most of what an attacker learns comes from public sources, certificate transparency, DNS and search engines — not from intrusion.
days.misconception: Confusing reconnaissance with attack. Passive gathering touches nothing; that distinction is what makes it legal and what makes it ethical.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/00_scope/09_scan_result_tally.py` — turn synthetic scan output into a tally using a rule **you** write down first, so the result is reproducible rather than vibes.
days.check: Say the five phases in order from memory (Day 2), then list what passive gathering can learn about a domain without touching it.
days.gate: List six passive sources you would check for a domain you own, and say what each can reveal.

days.title: Scanning: what a port state actually means
days.idea: Open, filtered and closed are statements about responses, not about services; enumeration turns a port into a version and a version into a known risk.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/02_access/05_config_audit.py` — compare a synthetic service table against a policy of what should be exposed. Enumerate, then judge.
days.gate: Explain to a non-technical owner why one open port can be unimportant and another can be urgent.

days.title: Traffic on the wire, and how detection sees you
days.idea: Cleartext protocols leak credentials; IDS/IPS signatures and anomaly baselines are what make noisy activity visible.
days.misconception: Thinking encryption is optional on a network you control. It is the cheapest control you have.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/01_detection/02_failed_login_summary.py` then `../security-exercises/exercises/01_detection/03_redact_secrets.py`. Redaction before collection: anything you capture is something you have to protect.
days.gate: Name three protocols that must never run in cleartext, and the mitigation for each.

days.title: Exploitation, payloads and the difference between proof and damage
days.idea: Proof of concept means demonstrating reachability with minimal impact — a callback, a file read — not taking a service down.
days.prerequisites: Days 2 and 4; a scope statement that names allowed actions.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/02_access/04_role_check.py`. Predict which requests the allow-list rejects before you run it; the assertions encode the least-privilege rule.
days.check: Day 5 (1 back), Day 3 (3 back), Day 1 (5 back — restate the law answer cold).
days.gate: Write the sentence you would put in a report when you proved access but chose not to escalate.

days.title: Web-based hacking: input you did not validate
days.idea: Injection, broken authentication and unsafe redirects all trace back to trusting client-supplied data.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/02_access/10_injection_guard.py` — allow-list plus parameterised query. Write the three inputs you think will break it, then let the test suite try.
days.gate: Explain parameterised queries to someone who has only ever written string SQL.

days.title: Wireless, plus a hard review of Days 1–7
days.idea: Wireless is another perimeter with its own failure modes: weak ciphers, captive portals, evil-twin networks.
days.practice: No new exercise. Re-solve `09_scan_result_tally.py` and `10_injection_guard.py` from a blank file with the solutions closed. Log every mistake you repeat — those are next week's recall cards.
days.check: Cold-write the one-sentence idea of Days 1–7. Only then open the pages. Anything missing becomes a day you repeat tomorrow.
days.gate: 90% of the recall prompts answered cold, or repeat this day instead of advancing.

days.title: Cryptography you can actually reason about
days.idea: Hashing proves integrity, symmetric encryption is fast for bulk data, asymmetric solves key distribution; hashing is not encryption.
days.misconception: Believing 'encrypted' means safe regardless of how the keys are stored or rotated.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/01_detection/11_hash_integrity.py` — hash a file, corrupt one byte, watch the verification fail. Then explain in your log why a hash is not encryption.
days.check: Day 8 (1 back), Day 6 (3 back), Day 2 (7 back).
days.gate: Explain to a friend why a leaked password database is dangerous even when hashed, and what raises the cost of cracking it.

days.title: How we take the bait: social engineering on yourself
days.idea: Urgency, authority and helpfulness bypass technical controls because they act on the person operating them.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/03_response/07_phishing_signals.py`. Then write the three lure patterns you are personally most vulnerable to and the one control that would catch each.
days.check: Day 9 (1 back), Day 7 (3 back), Day 3 (7 back).
days.gate: Draft a message you would flag as suspicious, and annotate every signal that gave it away.

days.title: The pen test: turning findings into a decision
days.idea: A report is triage: reproducible steps, honest severity with reasoning, and remediation someone can schedule.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/04_reporting/12_severity_scoring.py` then `../security-exercises/exercises/04_reporting/13_render_report.py`. The renderer refuses to produce a report without authorization evidence — keep that behaviour.
days.check: Day 10 (1 back), Day 8 (3 back), Day 4 (7 back).
days.gate: Show the report to someone who did not run the test; if they cannot say what to fix first, rewrite it.

days.title: Operational resilience: defending what you just learned to attack
days.idea: Resilience assumes breach. Detection, response and recovery are the skills that make an organisation safer than a list of patched CVEs.
days.practice: `../security-exercises/exercises/03_response/06_triage_finding.py` then `../security-exercises/exercises/03_response/08_incident_checklist.py`. Build the runbook for one finding from Day 11: who you call, what you shut down, what you prove afterwards.
days.check: Cold-write the ideas of Days 1–12. Anything missing returns to your retry queue. Then run the whole suite green.
days.gate: Present a five-minute brief: one asset, one realistic attack path, three controls, one thing you would monitor tonight.
